source.title: When Expressivity Meets Trainability: Fewer than $n$ Neurons Can Work
source.authors: Jia-Wei Zhang; Yu-Shun Zhang; Ming-Yi Hong; Ruoyu Sun; Z. Luo

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. The supplied text identifies the paper as NeurIPS 2021, while the record metadata says NeurIPS 2022.
record.tranche_reason: Reports training accuracy on random-labeled CIFAR-10 with a custom projected-gradient training regime, a different method and architecture from V1's convolutional SGD/Adam setting.
record.gate_note: The random-label experiment reports training accuracy in Table 3 and bears on V1's random-label memorization claim. The paper's synthetic regression training-loss results and CIFAR test-accuracy results do not measure a version's training-classification-error outcome. Its theoretical expressivity results establish existence of zero-loss solutions, not that gradient training reaches them.
record.test_reason: The random-label experiment measures training classification error, but uses fully connected one-hidden-layer networks and a custom constrained training regime. V1 specifies convolutional networks trained with SGD or Adam. The remaining results concern regression loss, expressivity, constrained optimization landscapes, or test accuracy and do not test V2–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate but needs qualifications. The authors establish zero-loss expressivity and an O(ε²) loss bound at constrained KKT points under their assumptions, while leaving convergence to such points for future work. Experiments favor their proposed regime for narrow networks. Random-label CIFAR-10 training accuracy is 98.72–99.98%; five of six settings exceed 99%.
record.recipe_differences: Uses mirrored LeCun initialization, a pairwise structure for output weights, and projected gradient descent on a constrained formulation; the comparison regime uses regular LeCun initialization and unconstrained GD-based methods. The random-label CIFAR-10 experiment uses a one-hidden-layer network.
record.method_sensitivity: On the random-labeled CIFAR-10 experiment, reported train accuracy varies with width and activation. In synthetic regression experiments, the authors state that the proposed regime performs well across tested widths, while regular unconstrained training fails when narrow and directly constraining regular training also fails when width and constraint size become small.

fits_no_version.finding: Constrained training of fully connected one-hidden-layer networks reaches 98.72–99.98% training accuracy on shuffled-label CIFAR-10 after 1000 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fully connected one-hidden-layer networks can nearly memorize random CIFAR-10 labels using mirrored initialization, paired output weights, and projected gradient training.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic tanh regression, regular training fails at small widths, while the proposed regime reaches low loss across tested widths and constraint sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A specially structured constrained training regime can improve optimization of narrow tanh regression networks.

fits_no_version.finding: For smooth activations under stated assumptions, the theory establishes zero-loss expressivity and approximate global optimality of constrained KKT points; algorithmic convergence remains unproved.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow smooth networks can have zero-loss solutions and a constrained formulation whose KKT points have small loss.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2021 (as stated in the supplied paper text; metadata gives Neural Information Processing Systems, 2022)
record.problems: The random-label CIFAR-10 experiment reports train accuracy but gives no uncertainty estimates or comparison baseline in Table 3. It uses a one-hidden-layer network and a custom constrained regime, so it does not directly establish the standard SGD/Adam convolutional result in V1. The authors note that ReLU is outside their theoretical analysis framework.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-linked rows omitted. Synthetic regression training losses are shown in Figure 4 without recoverable numeric values and do not measure classification training error; CIFAR and other real-data figures report test accuracy, not training classification error.

untested.parts: Training classification error of convolutional networks using SGD or Adam on CIFAR-10/100, including effects of width, label corruption, early stopping, and regularization.
Spurious-minimum frequencies in ReLU teacher-student problems and the effect of adding one or two student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts or special initialization.
Activation-matched signal and gradient propagation, training speed, trainable depth, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
Loss and curvature dynamics relative to learning-rate stability thresholds.
Training speed and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, including Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: The row states indicate inability to determine a listed version, not failure to memorize: Table 3 clearly demonstrates near-complete memorization in a different architecture and training regime. The synthetic experiments do not measure V2's teacher-student local-minimum frequencies, and the initialization changes do not test V4's signal-propagation or depth claims.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test SGD or Adam in the reported random-label CIFAR-10 experiment, convolutional networks, CIFAR-100, clean labels, or the effect of early stopping and regularization. The reported random-label experiment uses a one-hidden-layer network and the proposed constrained training regime.
